title: Adding the 200 day filter to an oversold SPY buy took the win rate to 85% and the return from 211% down to 28%
author: person-person12
selftext:
Every course teaches the same fix when a dip buy loses money, only buy the dip while price is above the 200 day average. I wanted to know what that filter actually does to the same rule rather than what its supposed to do, so I ran both versions over the same window in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading).

The rule both times: SPY daily candles, buy the close when RSI(14) is under 30, sell when RSI closes back above 50, no stop, no target, $10,000, Jan 2001 to Mar 2026. Commission and slippage charged on both sides.

**Plain version, no filter:**

* 140 trades
* 76.4% wins
* profit factor 2.19
* **up 211%**, $10,000 to $31,101
* max drawdown 31.4%

**Same rule, entries only while the close is above the 200 day:**

* 53 trades
* **84.9% wins**
* profit factor 1.59
* **up 27.8%**, $10,000 to $12,783
* max drawdown 32.7%

So the filter did the one thing its fans promise, the win rate went up 8 points, and almost every other number got worse. The return fell by a factor of seven and the drawdown came out slightly deeper than the version with no filter at all, which I did not expect from something sitting in cash most of the decade.

The reason is in the trade list. The filter throws out 87 of the 140 trades and theyre not a random 87, theyre every entry where price was under the 200 day, which is every panic in the sample. The filtered version has no trade at all between June 2007 and June 2009. It sat out the crash and the first leg of the recovery, and those were the biggest winners the plain rule ever got.

Its a bit like refusing to look at a house unless the street is already going up in price. You avoid the bad street and you also never get the cheap one.

Both versions still finished behind just holding SPY across the same window, and the plain one is the cleaner warning of the two, **76% of its trades won** and it came in behind anyway.

comments.author: read_more_comments
comments.body: It might not be a bad filter for an individual symbol, but I personally wouldn't wait for it to go over the 200 on an ETF like VOO. The bigger the dip, the bigger the discount, because I don't think the entire S&P stays down or goes bankrupt.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Agreed, and the numbers back you up here. Waiting for the 200 took the win rate to 85% and the return down to 28%, so it paid for a **cleaner looking hit rate with almost all of the upside.** Buying the dip deeper with no filter was the better of the two by a wide margin.

replies.author: SuperOrbital_Trading
replies.body: This is the most Chatgpt answer I have ever seen. Even has the bold text in the middle of the sentence.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: The filter took the win rate to 85% and dropped the return from 211% to 28%, which is **the entire point of the post** and is either right or it isnt. Which part of it do you think is wrong?

replies.author: SuperOrbital_Trading
replies.body: Give me a recipe to make a grilled cheese special.

comments.author: Primary-Ad9481
comments.body: I have been paying for historical data down to 1m and have claude backtest all algo and all tradingview strategy. All of them come back that buying SPY and hold no matter when will always beat anything else.  Depressing.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Its less depressing once you notice its SPY specifically. Youre benchmarking every rule against the thing with a century of upward drift baked into it, so the rule has to beat the drift and pay its costs on top. The same rules on single names or futures dont have that headwind, theyre just harder in other ways.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Correct, and thats the whole post. 85% of the trades won and the return went from 211% to 28%.

comments.author: MrKittyCatMeowFace03
comments.body: max DD 31.4% , on SPY? That sounds a bit wild.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Its not wild for a rule thats long SPY with no exit. SPY itself drew down 55% in 2008 and 34% in 2020, so anything holding through those wears most of it. Fair question on which one though, im not going to guess at it from memory, ill pull the curve and check.

comments.author: Benostalgi
comments.body: Doesn’t this mean that if you only took trades below the 200 then those 87 trades would return around 85% (about 18500?). Almost 3x better! Still not great for the time period but seems to imply that a 200 ma filter produces better results when used in the opposite way to what we are frequently advised.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Youre right on the direction, so I went and ran it rather than guess. Same rule, same window, same costs, only the entries where price closed **below** the 200 day: 105 trades, 71.4% wins, finished up **137.1%** at $23,713, profit factor 1.94, worst drawdown 29.3%.

So its not the 85% you get by subtracting one from the other, because each version compounds on its own equity and the trade counts dont split cleanly. But the point holds, the below-200 half is carrying nearly all of the return and the filter throws it away.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Not quite. The returns don't split that way. The 211% and 28% figures are compounded, so the gap between them isn't the return of the other 87 trades. Trade order and position sizing matter, and a big early gain changes what later trades compound on. The only way to know what those 87 trades did is to run the below-200-only version separately.

Also check three things before reading it as "the filter works backwards":

* **Independent episodes, not trades.** Those 87 entries are probably clustered in a few panics (2002, 2008-09, 2020, 2022). A cluster of RSI<30 signals in one selloff is really one bet, so your effective sample may be closer to 5-8 events than 87.
* **Drawdown.** With no stop, buying below the 200 in 2008 means sitting through a lot of further downside. The filtered version's max drawdown was already slightly deeper than the unfiltered one, so the below-200 version could look worse on risk than the return suggests.
* **Regime dependence.** It mostly measures "did the market recover after a crash," which is a handful of macro shocks. Splitting results by what caused the selloff would show whether it's a repeatable pattern or two or three lucky V-shapes.

Cymetica's EventTrader tags macro and corporate events with point-in-time context, which could help label those clusters (Lehman, COVID, rate shocks) so you can see which ones drive the result.

I'd run the inverse filter, report time in market and per-episode returns, and compare to buy-and-hold on a risk-adjusted basis. Then freeze the rule and forward test it, because a filter chosen after seeing this backtest is already overfit to it.
